chapter_title: Concerning the Garment of the Waters: how great is

fills.notes: Keeps the didactic, impersonal teacherly cadence of the substrate: reference back to an earlier correspondential explanation (how the rulers ingest an element and it becomes torment).

fills.fill: before, that they could not be filled
fills.notes: The logic requires an explicit point: the rulers consume the water yet remain insatiable; this sets up ¶7 (“as they shall not … to a single stomach, to their fill”).
Bridges from “Many waters poured forth” to the cosmological effect (“the rivers flow”): the rivers are the outflow/effect of those waters.
Needs a verb to connect “The mouth of the rulers … those …”: in the substrate, the ‘mouth’ is the receiving/ingesting organ; it ‘opens’ to draw in the element.
Correspondentially fits with mouth/stomach imagery and the theme of devouring rulers; also prepares for ¶7’s “descent to its stomach.”
Restores a minimal grammatical link: “the warriors of destruction … laboured and brought them forth” needs a subject-conjunction tying rulers/warriors to the action.
Required by sense: the seven rivers flow into each mouth “as they shall not be gathered to a single stomach” (i.e., not consolidated; each ruler has its own intake).
Completes the simile: “like the bellies of …” matches the imagery of mouth/stomach, and describes capacious, never-emptied receptacles.
Old substrate regularly casts the devouring powers as serpent-forms; “bellies of serpents” coheres with insatiable ingestion and underworld physiology.
Parallel to “rain”: “rain and mist fed their existent days” (i.e., continual supply sustaining their state). Keeps natural correspondences (rain/mist) as influxes.
The paragraph resumes by pointing to what has just been described (the waters/rivers and their torment), so a deictic “This is how great…” fits the didactic register.
Requires a verb of encompassing/holding: the struggle ‘has bound up’ or ‘has constrained’ the destructive creatures (continuing “entwined, bound…”).
Completes the triad “entwined, bound, and …”: the substrate idea is containment/immurement of the giants within the structure of the world.
The concealment is temporal: they are hidden from common flesh “until the end” (i.e., until the dissolution). Matches ensuing cosmic dissolution language.
Supplies the copula/auxiliary needed: “These rulers shall be revealed.” Revelation here is cosmological disclosure at the final unbinding, not devotional.
The universe of flesh is destroyed/dissolved; “in that dissolution” anchors the clause in the same event and keeps the impersonal, process-focused tone.
Natural-effects language: “all pass away with its forms” (i.e., the formed appearances of fleshly cosmos). Fits the substrate’s emphasis on forms as ultimates.
Sets the proportion: the visible stream is “as nothing” compared to the immeasurable hidden waters; matches the comparative rhetoric of ¶10.
Imperative in teaching mode: “See … and be amazed” commonly has a preceding “look/consider” to direct attention to correspondential measure.
Grammar and sense: “the one whom these waters are lesser than” (i.e., even these vast waters are less than that god’s power/measure). Keeps cosmological scaling.

assessment: Most gaps are constrained by the internal physiological-cosmological sequence (mouth → descent → stomach → burning; outflow → rivers; concealment → final revelation/dissolution). Several places (¶6 #8; ¶7 #3–5; ¶9 #7) remain only moderately/tentatively recoverable because multiple synonymous images could fit (throats/gullets; bellies/jaws; rain/dew/mist; forms/figures), but the underlying correspondential logic—insatiable ingestion, punitive descent, and cosmic containment until the final dissolution—strongly determines the kind of wording required.
